name: Dopamine / porn avoidance

card.summary: Abstaining from porn, masturbation or other stimulation to 'reset' dopamine, popular in self-improvement circles; claimed benefits lack supporting evidence per researchers.
card.note: Researchers say prolonged abstinence may worsen existing mental health problems; the NoFap community has been linked by scholars to manosphere ideas.

quick.overview:
This practice covers avoiding pornography, masturbation and other highly stimulating habits, with the aim of improving focus, confidence, attractiveness or mood. Communities such as NoFap and the 'dopamine fasting' trend frame it as resetting the brain's reward system.

In looksmaxxing circles, abstaining is often listed as a free self-improvement step alongside fitness and skincare. Proponents describe benefits such as willpower and confidence, while researchers report little supporting evidence.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say removing high-stimulation activities reduces impulsive behaviour and restores sensitivity to ordinary rewards. The psychologist who developed dopamine fasting, Cameron Sepah, has said the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviours rather than literally lower dopamine. Critics note that dopamine is vital and that avoiding a stimulus does not reset it.
quick.risks: Surveys found members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than to abstinence, and some researchers argue prolonged abstinence may worsen distress. Extreme versions such as sensory deprivation are criticised by clinicians. DSM-5-TR does not recognise porn addiction.

lead: Dopamine and porn avoidance is a self-improvement practice in which people step back from pornography, masturbation, short-form video, gaming and similar high-stimulation habits. Practitioners use it as a way to look and present better: the freed-up time and energy goes into the gym, walking, skincare routines and sleep, and followers describe feeling more confident, more focused and more motivated to keep up appearance-related habits [1][2][3].

Two overlapping movements are involved. NoFap is an online community founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread, and dopamine fasting was developed by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a cognitive behavioural tool for impulsive behaviours [1][2]. On looksmax.org, members announce short detoxes (for example, ten days without short-form video or masturbation paired with more daily steps and a topical routine) as a way to reset mood and restart training momentum [3].

Wikipedia reports that the most prominent claimed benefits of NoFap lack supporting evidence and that experts describe many of its views as simplistic [1]. Regarding dopamine fasting, neuroscientists have criticised the idea of a dopamine reset, and Sepah says the goal is reducing impulsive behaviours rather than lowering dopamine itself [2]. Some forum authors make the same point, describing their own detox plans as reducing artificial highs rather than removing dopamine [4].

chain: Cut out high-stimulation habits for a set period
Time and energy shift toward training, sleep and grooming
More consistent routines and a more confident presentation
angle.text: Practitioners use abstinence and screen breaks to free up time and attention for the habits that shape appearance, such as lifting, walking and skincare, and many report feeling more confident and driven. Some also hold that abstaining raises testosterone or attractiveness directly, a claim researchers do not support.

infobox: Porn addiction not recognised in DSM-5-TR

paras: Versions range from narrow (no pornography or masturbation) to broad (also no social media, gaming, junk food or notifications). One widely shared looksmax.org guide stresses that a detox is not about cutting out dopamine but about reducing artificial highs, and suggests lighter measures such as limiting social media, keeping the phone out of the bedroom and avoiding screens in the first hour of the morning, replaced by exercise, reading and time outdoors [4]. Others pair a short detox with fitness targets, such as higher daily step counts and a set weekly routine for a skincare or hair device [3].

NoFap began as a subreddit in 2011 after a thread about a 2003 study claiming testosterone rose after seven days of abstinence; that study was retracted in 2021 [1]. Rhodes later built NoFap.com, which reports about 1.2 million users as of August 2025 [1]. Dopamine fasting originated with California psychologist Cameron Sepah as a CBT-based approach to impulsive behaviours and is often described as a Silicon Valley trend [2].

NoFap members cite improved relationships, willpower and mental clarity; goals vary among members [1]. Dopamine fasting proponents say it builds self-discipline, with versions ranging from avoiding online technology to broader abstention [2]. In looksmaxxing forums the practice is also bundled with claims about testosterone, confidence and attractiveness, and some threads discuss dopamine receptor pharmacology and supplements aimed at boosting dopamine [5].

A 2020 study found motivation to abstain was linked to viewing masturbation as unhealthy, religiosity, conservatism and lower trust in science, and a 2021 qualitative study found that framing abstinence around relapse appeared to sustain distress [1]. A 2023 preregistered survey by Prause and Binnie reported that members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than abstinence [1]. Psychologist David Ley and therapist Paula Hall say there is little medical evidence for claimed physical benefits [1]. The DSM-5-TR does not recognise porn addiction, and ICD-11 classifies compulsive sexual behaviour as an impulse control disorder [1].

On dopamine fasting, Peter Grinspoon called Sepah's work sensible but not groundbreaking, while neuroscientist Ciara McCabe disputes the idea of resetting the brain by avoiding dopamine triggers [2]. A 2022 paper in Lifestyle Medicine considered whether it is maladaptive or misunderstood [2]. Neuroscience reviews describe dopamine as involved in learning, motivation and movement rather than simply pleasure, which is why researchers say the term 'reset' does not map onto the brain's biology [6].

No controlled clinical trials of porn or dopamine avoidance as a looksmaxxing or appearance intervention were found. Related observational and survey research on NoFap members and screen-time impulsivity exists [1][2].

Researchers say prolonged abstinence framed around relapse may sustain distress in some people [1]. Journalists and researchers have criticised some forum content as misogynistic and scholars have linked the community to the manosphere; Rhodes has also been involved in litigation against researchers [1].

timeline.event: A study on testosterone after abstinence that later inspired NoFap is published [1].
NoFap founded as a subreddit by Alexander Rhodes [1].
The 2003 study that inspired NoFap is retracted [1].
Prause and Binnie survey reports on NoFap members' mental health [1].

lore.intro: Abstaining from porn and stimulation is commonly mentioned in looksmaxxing communities as a free step alongside fitness and skincare, with detox threads ranging from short screen breaks to multi-day abstinence challenges [3][4].

claims.claim: Abstaining resets dopamine and increases confidence, focus and attractiveness
claims.believers: Proponents cite willpower, better mood at the gym and renewed motivation, and some posters announce short detoxes to restart their routine [3][4].
claims.experts: Researchers say the claimed benefits lack supporting evidence and that dopamine cannot be reset by avoiding stimuli [1][2][6].

claims.believers: A Reddit thread about a 2003 study claimed a testosterone spike after seven days [1].

claims.claim: Reducing phone and short-form video use frees time and focus for self-improvement
claims.believers: Forum guides list reels, gaming and notifications as attention drains and recommend replacing them with exercise, reading and sunlight [4].
claims.experts: No published trials have tested a dopamine detox as an appearance intervention; Sepah describes the approach as a behavioural tool for impulsivity [2].
